newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-ALBANIAN COACH COPES WITH DWINDLING SQUAD.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ALBANIAN COACH COPES WITH DWINDLING SQUAD.

text.p: Albanian soccer coach Sulejman Mema has more on his mind than simple matters such as tactics or what team to pick at the Mediterranean Games in southern Italy.

With 13 players seeking political asylum abroad and the domestic league suspended amid unrest in Albania this year, Mema has been expending most of his energies on rebuilding the team and preventing further desertions.

"In November last year we had built a good side. But then 12 players asked for asylum in Spain," he said at a training session before Albania played hosts Italy on Thursday in a competition between under-23 teams.
Italy won 4-0, with around 200 Albanian spectators brought in by bus from refugee camps in southern Italy.
Eight under-21 players, a physiotherapist and the suspended general secretary of the Albanian Football Association are still in Spain after matches there in April.

All refused to return to Albania after their home games were moved to the Spanish town of Granada because the political situation in the impoverished Balkan nation was deemed too dangerous for visiting teams.

A further five Albanians deserted the team after a 1-1 draw with Portugal in May, leaving Mema with only two members of the original squad which played their last real home match six months ago in a 3-2 victory over Armenia in the capital Tirana.
Albania slid into chaos in March with the outbreak of violence in large parts of the south following the collapse of dubious investment schemes.
Mema said it was hard to convince his players not to see the trip to Italy as a chance to escape the turmoil but added he was certain no-one would leave the squad this time.
"It is difficult to change the mentality of these players. But I don't think they will seek political asylum here.
"We want to return because after the elections something will change for sure," he said. Albania has general elections on June 29 to try to restore political order.

Speaking at the squad's training ground near the Adriatic coast, where over 16,000 Albanian refugees have flooded into Italy this year on a flotilla of rusty boats, Mema said many of the team had not played competitive soccer this year.
Striker Elton Marini, who lives near the port of Vlore in the rebel-held south, said he had trained by himself and with friends after the collapse of the Albanian league.
In contrast to the flashy lifestyle of Italian serie A footballers, the Albanians paid their own ferry fares to Bari.
The only players with top-level experience are attacking midfielder Edi Martini and defender Adrian Dhashi, who are both with German side Frankfurt.
They are the only remaining Albanians from the national under-21 side as it was before the defections.
With foreign deals already reached, neither needed to seek asylum in Spain.

Martini, who signed a three-year contract this year after a season with Austrian side Klagenfurt, was pessimistic for the future of the national side despite his own dramatic rise to the Bundesliga from Albanian club Skuderi.
"The Albanians are the most unfortunate people in Europe, also in football," he said. "But I am Albanian. Playing for the national side makes me proud."

Albanian soccer has had many similar tribulations in the past. In the late 1970s, European governing body UEFA banned the country's clubs from competing after the late dictator Enver Hoxha refused to let Tirana travel to Moscow for a cup match.
Hoxha, who died in 1985, had recently switched his communist allegiance from Moscow to Beijing. For five years the national squad did not travel outside Albania on the regime's orders.
Mema dismissed recent Italian newspaper reports suggesting Albanian soccer teams were politically aligned.

A recent match between northern Tirana and southern Vlore was depicted as a battle between supporters of President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party and the opposition Socialists, who head the national unity government installed in March.
"Sport doesn't enter into politics. The players here are from the south and the north," Mema said.
He said sport had the potential to unite the nation.
"We are living in poverty. We are doing everything to survive. Let's hope that those in charge of sports can do something to help the country grow.".

"Other (organised) sporting activities don't exist now. Everyone will go to the televisions to watch our games. It is important to give something good to these people who are suffering at the moment."
Bashkim Koka, the squad's second coach, had decided to make a direct impression by standing as a non-aligned candidate in the elections. He could be sure of some support.
"I'm going to vote for Bashkim because he's an honest person," said Mema.
